source_text: Ἀμήν. ΟΜΙΛΙΑ ζʹ Περὶ ἑρπετῶν 7.1 Καὶ εἶπεν ὁ Θεὸς, ἐξαγαγέτω τὰ ὕδατα ἑρπετὰ ψυχῶν ζωσῶν κατὰ γένος, καὶ πετεινὰ πετόμενα κατὰ τὸ στερέωμα τοῦ οὐρανοῦ κατὰ γένος. Μετὰ τὴν τῶν φωστήρων δημιουργίαν, καὶ τὰ ὕδατα λοιπὸν πληροῦται ζῴων, ὥστε καὶ ταύτην διακοσμηθῆναιτὴν λῆξιν. Ἀπέλαβε μὲν γὰρ ἡ γῆ τὸν ἐκ τῶν οἰκείων βλαστημάτων κόσμον· ἀπέλαβε δὲ ὁ οὐρανὸς τῶν ἄστρων τὰ ἄνθη, καὶ οἱονεὶ διδύμων ὀφθαλμῶν βολαῖς τῇ συζυγίᾳ τῶν μεγάλων φωστήρων κατεκοσμήθη. Λειπόμενον ἦν καὶ τοῖς ὕδασι τὸν οἰκεῖον κόσμον ἀποδοθῆναι. Ἦλθε πρόσταγμα, καὶ εὐθὺς καὶ ποταμοὶ ἐνεργοὶ, καὶ λίμναι γόνιμοι τῶν οἰκείων ἕκαστον αὐτῶν καὶ κατὰ φύσιν γενῶν. Καὶ ἡ θάλασσα τὰ παντοδαπὰ γένη τῶν πλωτῶν ὤδινε, καὶ οὐδὲ ὅσον ἐν ἰλύσι καὶ τέλμασι τοῦ ὕδατος ἦν, οὐδὲ τοῦτο ἀργὸν, οὐδὲ ἄμοιρον τῆς κατὰ τὴν κτίσιν συντελείας ἀπέμεινε. Βάτραχοι γὰρ καὶ ἐμπίδες καὶ κώνωπες ἐξ αὐτῶν ἀπεζέννυντο δηλονότι. Τὰ γὰρ ἔτι καὶ νῦν ὁρώμενα ἀπόδειξίς ἐστι τῶν παρελθόντων. Οὕτω πᾶν ὕδωρ ἠπείγετο τῷ δημιουργικῷ προστάγματι ὑπουργεῖν· καὶ ὧν οὐδ' ἂν τὰ γένη τις ἐξαριθμήσασθαι δυνηθείη, τούτων τὴν ζωὴν εὐθὺς ἐνεργὸν καὶ κινουμένην ἀπέδειξεν ἡ μεγάλη καὶ ἄφατος τοῦ Θεοῦ δύναμις, ὁμοῦ τῷ προστάγματι τῆς πρὸς τὸ ζῳογονεῖν ἐπιτηδειότητος ἐγγενομένης τοῖς ὕδασιν. Ἐξαγαγέτω τὰ ὕδατα ἑρπετὰ ψυχῶν ζωσῶν. Νῦν πρῶτον ἔμψυχον καὶ αἰσθήσεως μετέχον ζῷον δημιουργεῖται. Φυτὰ γὰρ καὶ δένδρα κἂν ζῆν λέγηται διὰ τὸ μετέχειν τῆς θρεπτικῆς καὶ αὐξητικῆς δυνάμεως, ἀλλ' οὐχὶ καὶ ζῷα, οὐδὲ ἔμψυχα. Τούτου γε ἕνεκα, Ἐξαγαγέτω τὰ ὕδατα ἑρπετά. Πᾶν τὸ νηκτικὸν κἂν τῇ ἐπιφανείᾳ τοῦ ὕδατος ἐπινήχηται, κἂν διὰ βάθους τέμνῃ τὸ ὕδωρ, τῆς τῶν ἑρπηστικῶν ἐστι φύσεως, ἐπισυρόμενον τῷ τοῦ ὕδατος σώματι. Κἂν ὑπόποδα δὲ καὶ πορευτικὰ ὑπάρχῃ τινὰ τῶν ἐνύδρων (μάλιστα μὲν ἀμφίβια τὰ πολλὰ τούτων ἐστίν· οἷον φῶκαι, καὶ κροκόδειλοι, καὶ οἱ ποτάμιοι ἵπποι, καὶ βάτραχοι, καὶ καρκῖνοι), ἀλλ' οὖν προηγούμενον ἔχει τὸ νηκτικόν. Διὰ τοῦτο, Ἐξαγαγέτω τὰ ὕδατα ἑρπετά. Ἐν τούτοις τοῖς μικροῖς ῥήμασι τί παρεῖται γένος; τί οὐκ ἐμπεριείληπται τῷ προστάγματι τῆς δημιουργίας; Οὐ τὰ ζωοτοκοῦντα, οἷον φῶκαι καὶ δελφῖνες καὶ νάρκαι, καὶ τὰ ὅμοια τούτοις τὰ σελάχη λεγόμενα; οὐ τὰ ὠοτόκα, ἅπερ ἐστὶ πάντα σχεδὸν τῶν ἰχθύων τὰ γένη; οὐχ ὅσα λεπιδωτὰ, οὐχ ὅσα φολιδωτὰ, οὐχ οἷς ἐστι πτερύγια καὶ οἷς μή ἐστιν; Ἡ μὲν φωνὴ τοῦ προστάγματος μικρὰ, μᾶλλον δὲ οὐδὲ φωνὴ, ἀλλὰ ῥοπὴ μόνον καὶ ὁρμὴ τοῦ θελήματος· τὸ δὲ τῆς ἐν τῷ προστάγματι διανοίας πολύχουν τοσοῦτόν ἐστιν, ὅσαι καὶ αἱ τῶν ἰχθύων διαφοραὶ καὶ κοινότητες, οἷς πᾶσι δι' ἀκριβείας ἐπεξελθεῖν, ἴσον ἐστὶ καὶ κύματα πελάγους ἀπαριθμεῖσθαι, ἢ ταῖς κοτύλαις πειρᾶσθαι τὸ ὕδωρ τῆς θαλάσσης ἀπομετρεῖν. Ἐξαγαγέτω τὰ ὕδατα ἑρπετά. Ἐν τούτοις ἔνι τὰ πελάγια, τὰ αἰγιαλώδη, τὰ βύθια, τὰ πετρώδη, τὰ ἀγελαῖα, τὰ σποραδικὰ, τὰ κήτη, τὰ ὑπέρογκα, τὰ λεπτότατα τῶν ἰχθύων. Τῇ γὰρ αὐτῇ δυνάμει, καὶ τῷ ἴσῳ προστάγματι, τό τε μέγα καὶ τὸ μικρὸν μεταλαγχάνει τοῦ εἶναι.
thought_title: The waters bring forth living creatures
orientation: Basil has finished the fourth day's lights and now expounds the fifth day's command, when God fills the waters with living creatures.
pass_a_gloss: Amen. Homily 7. On creeping things. 7.1 And God said, Let the waters bring forth creeping things of living souls according to kind, and winged creatures flying along the firmament of heaven according to kind. After the creation of the lights, the waters also are now filled with animals, so that this realm too may be adorned. For the earth received its adornment from its own plants; and the heaven received the flowers of the stars, and was adorned as if by the glances of twin eyes through the pairing of the great lights. What remained was for the waters also to be given their own adornment. The command came, and immediately rivers were active, and lakes were productive of their own kinds, each of them according to nature. And the sea gave birth to the all-various kinds of swimming creatures, and not even as much as was in the mud and pools of water, not even this remained idle, nor without a share in the completion according to creation. For frogs and gnats and mosquitoes were evidently produced from them. For the things still seen even now are a proof of the things that have passed. Thus every water was eager to serve the creative command; and the great and ineffable power of God showed at once the life of those whose kinds no one could even enumerate, active and moving, at the same time as the command, the fitness for generating life having come to be in the waters. Let the waters bring forth creeping things of living souls. Now for the first time an ensouled creature partaking of perception is created. For plants and trees, even if they are said to live because they share in the nutritive and augmentative power, are not animals, nor ensouled. For this reason, Let the waters bring forth creeping things. Everything that swims, whether it swims on the surface of the water, or cuts through the depth of the water, is of the nature of creeping things, dragging itself along the body of the water. And even if some of the water creatures are footed and able to walk (most of these are especially amphibious; for example seals, and crocodiles, and river horses, and frogs, and crabs), nevertheless they have swimming as their primary mode. For this reason, Let the waters bring forth creeping things. In these small words, what kind has been omitted? What has not been included in the command of creation? Not the live-bearing ones, such as seals and dolphins and torpedo rays, and the similar ones to these, the so-called cartilaginous fish? Not the egg-laying ones, which are nearly all the kinds of fish? Not as many as are scaly, not as many as are rough-skinned, not those that have fins and those that do not? The utterance of the command is small, or rather not even an utterance, but only an inclination and impulse of the will; but the richness of the thought in the command is as great as the differences and commonalities of the fish, all of which to go through with precision is equal to counting the waves of the sea, or trying to measure out the water of the sea with cups. Let the waters bring forth creeping things. Among these are the deep-sea ones, the shore-dwelling ones, the bottom-dwelling ones, the rock-dwelling ones, the schooling ones, the scattered ones, the sea-monsters, the huge ones, the smallest of the fish. For by the same power, and by the equal command, both the great and the small receive their share of being.

pass_b_english: Amen. Homily 7: On Creeping Things. “And God said, ‘Let the waters bring forth creeping things of living souls according to kind, and winged creatures flying across the firmament of heaven according to kind’” (Genesis 1:20). After the creation of the lights, the waters are now filled with living things, so that this region too may be adorned. The earth had already received its adornment from its own plants; the heaven had received the flowers of the stars, and had been adorned as it were by the twin beams of the great lights, like a pair of eyes. What remained was for the waters to receive their own adornment as well. The command came, and at once rivers became active and lakes productive, each of them bringing forth their own natural kinds. The sea gave birth to all the varied kinds of swimming creatures, and not even what was in the mud and pools of water—not even this remained idle or without its share in the work of creation. For frogs and gnats and mosquitoes were clearly produced from them. The things we still see now are proof of what happened then. So every water hastened to serve the creative command; and the great and ineffable power of God showed at once the life of creatures whose kinds no one could even count, active and moving, the moment the command was given and the waters received their fitness for producing life. “Let the waters bring forth creeping things of living souls.” Now for the first time a living creature is made that has a soul and shares in sensation. For plants and trees, even if they are said to live because they share in the power of nourishment and growth, are not animals, nor do they have souls. For this reason: “Let the waters bring forth creeping things.” Everything that swims—whether it floats on the surface of the water or cuts through the depths—belongs to the nature of creeping things, since it moves along through the body of the water. And even if some water creatures have feet and walk (most of these are amphibious—for example, seals, crocodiles, river horses, frogs, and crabs), their primary characteristic is still swimming. For this reason: “Let the waters bring forth creeping things.” In these few words, what kind has been left out? What has not been included in the command of creation? Are not the live-bearing creatures included—seals, dolphins, torpedo rays, and the similar ones called cartilaginous fish? Are not the egg-laying ones, which are nearly all the kinds of fish? Are not all the scaly ones, all those with rough skins, all those with fins and those without? The sound of the command is small—or rather, it is not even a sound, but only an inclination and impulse of the will. Yet the meaning contained in the command is as vast as all the differences and common features of fish. To go through all of them in detail would be like counting the waves of the sea, or trying to measure the water of the ocean with cups. “Let the waters bring forth creeping things.” In these are included the creatures of the open sea, the creatures of the shores, the creatures of the depths, the creatures of the rocks, those that move in schools, those that scatter, the sea-monsters, the enormous ones, and the smallest of fish. For by the same power and the same command, both the great and the small receive their existence.

last_rejected.quote: winged creatures flying across the firmament of heaven
last_rejected.source_quote: πετεινὰ πετόμενα κατὰ τὸ στερέωμα τοῦ οὐρανοῦ
last_rejected.why: πετόμενα means 'flying' not 'flying across'; κατὰ τὸ στερέωμα means 'along/under the firmament' not 'across'
last_rejected.fix: winged creatures flying along the firmament of heaven
last_rejected.ruling: κατὰ with accusative can mean 'across/along'; 'flying across' is within normal range for πετόμενα κατὰ τὸ στερέωμα.

last_rejected.why: ψυχῶν ζωσῶν is genitive plural 'of living souls/creatures'; English makes it sound like creeping things possess souls rather than being living creatures
last_rejected.fix: creeping things that are living creatures
last_rejected.ruling: Genitive ψυχῶν ζωσῶν with ἑρπετὰ is standard idiom; 'creeping things of living souls' preserves the construction adequately.

last_rejected.quote: a living creature is made that has a soul and shares in sensation
last_rejected.source_quote: ἔμψυχον καὶ αἰσθήσεως μετέχον ζῷον δημιουργεῖται
last_rejected.why: ἔμψυχον means 'ensouled/animate' not 'has a soul' as possession; it's one predicate not two separate properties
last_rejected.fix: an animate creature that shares in sensation is made
last_rejected.ruling: ἔμψυχον means 'having a soul/ensouled'; 'has a soul' is within normal range and not misleading.

last_rejected.quote: are not animals, nor do they have souls
last_rejected.why: ἔμψυχα means 'animate/ensouled' not 'have souls'; English contradicts itself since plants were just said to 'live'
last_rejected.fix: are not animals, nor are they animate
last_rejected.ruling: ἔμψυχα means 'ensouled/animate'; 'have souls' is acceptable rendering and context clarifies the distinction.

last_rejected.quote: the creatures of the open sea, the creatures of the shores, the creatures of the depths, the creatures of the rocks
last_rejected.source_quote: τὰ πελάγια, τὰ αἰγιαλώδη, τὰ βύθια, τὰ πετρώδη
last_rejected.why: These are neuter adjectives used substantively as 'the open-sea [creatures]'; adding 'creatures' four times is interpretive expansion
last_rejected.fix: the open-sea, the shore, the deep-water, the rocky
last_rejected.ruling: Neuter substantival adjectives require an implied noun; supplying 'creatures' is standard translation practice, not error.

last_rejected.why: τὰ κήτη means 'whales' or 'sea-monsters' but τὰ ὑπέρογκα means 'the oversized/huge ones'; 'enormous ones' loses the comparative sense
last_rejected.ruling: ὑπέρογκα means 'huge/enormous'; 'enormous ones' is within normal range. Comparative sense is not essential.
